newsitem.title: CONGO: No Zaire deal but fresh talks, rebels to fight on.
newsitem.headline: No Zaire deal but fresh talks, rebels to fight on.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko offered at talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Sunday to hand power to an elected president.
But Kabila said his forces, reported to be within 100 km (60 miles) of Kinshasa and advancing, would fight on while Mobutu considered his demand that he resign.
The civil war rivals, meeting for the first time on a customised South African icebreaker in Congo, failed to agree on the terms of Mobutu's departure.

South African President Nelson Mandela, who hosted the meeting on SAS Outeniqua, told a closing news conference that he would convene a fresh round of talks in eight to 10 days to "narrow the gap between the two parties".

"I made it clear a ceasefire is out of the question and my forces will continue to advance on all fronts. If we make it to Kinshasa before the eight days then too bad but we cannot wait while he makes up his mind," Kabila told Reuters by telephone from the ship in Congo's port of Pointe Noire.
Residents, contacted from Kinshasa, said that rebels advancing rapidly in trucks were under 100 km (60 miles) of the teeming capital, well within striking distance. The city itself was calm.
In northeastern Zaire, dozens of Rwandan Hutu refugees suffocated or were crushed to death on Sunday in a train carrying them from a refugee camp to be repatriated by air, witnesses said.

Aid workers and journalists saw dozens of bodies of refugees tumbling from open railway carriages as the train pulled into Kisangani station. An official of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said he estimated more than 100 people had died in the crush.

Aboard the South African ship, U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, reading the final statement, told the news conference that Mobutu had offered to hand over to an elected president.
Kabila, for his part, insisted that his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire should act as the transitional authority to organise elections.
Witnesses said Mobutu left the ship immediately after the closing news conference. His destination was unclear. Kabila aides said the rebel leader planned to return to Angola.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated the sprawling yet mineral-rich nation at the heart of Africa for more than three decades.

He was among a handful of world leaders such as the late Shah of Iran, the late President Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines and Chile's Augusto Pinochet who were propped up by the United States as bulwarks against Soviet communism.
Battling cancer and the whirlwind revolt at home, he looked grim-faced and sad as he boarded the SAS Outeniqua where Kabila and Mandela had been waiting for him since late Saturday.
Kabila, by contrast, looked relaxed and smiled broadly as he entered the closing news conference.
Kabila, 56, told Reuters his forces, who took up arms in October and control three quarters of the sprawling nation at the heart of Africa, would fight on.

"Mobutu has asked me to give him eight days while he considers our demand to resign. I have agreed to that request and we shall meet again on this same ship within the next eight days. But I have told him and the mediators that there will be no ceasefire while he considers our demands," he said.
One diplomat said the rebel leader had been looking for any excuse not to come. At one point, a frustrated Mandela got on the satellite phone to him in Angola and shouted down the line.

Mobutu, wearing his trade-mark leopard-skin hat, boarded the ship with great difficulty on Friday, when talks were originally planned. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board up a ramp.
On Sunday, he and his wife Bobi Ladawa squeezed into a makeshift quayside lift and were hoisted on board.
He clutched Bobi Ladawa's hand. In his other hand, he gripped his usual carved walking stick.

Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of fighting alongside Kabila's forces. Independent sources say rebels have captured Mobutu's Lisala birthplace and are marching on Kinshasa and his jungle palace in Gbadolite in the north.

Kabila said he expected his forces to be 80 km (50 miles) from Kinshasa by Sunday evening. Residents said the rebels were massing fighters in Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa, for a final assault on the city of five million people.
The military governor of Kinshasa urged residents to stay calm in the face of the rebel advance and told security forces to protect its population without discrimination.
The U.S. State Department urged American citizens to leave Zaire and warned them not to travel there citing the "deteriorating security and political situation".
The United States, France, former colonial power Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
